4.title: Stewards of Grace: The Meaning of Suffering
4.overview: Chapter 4 returns to suffering in the light of the end: “The end of all things is at hand” (v. 7). The first half (vv. 1–11) shows how suffering settles a believer’s break with the old life, and how a church facing the end should live: clear-headed for prayer, loving earnestly, hospitable, and using every gift for others. The second half (vv. 12–19) speaks directly to the fiery trial: do not be surprised; rejoice to share Christ’s sufferings; do not be ashamed to suffer as a Christian; and entrust your soul to a faithful Creator.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Stewards of God's Varied Grace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Since Christ suffered, arm yourselves with the same mind: suffering for him settles our break with sin. You have spent enough time living as pagans do; your old friends are puzzled and slander you, but they will answer to God. The end is near, so be clear-headed for prayer, love one another deeply, show hospitality without grumbling, and use each gift to serve others, so that God is glorified through Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
Stewards of God's Varied Grace

Suffering for Christ settles a believer's break with sin. Because the end is near, stay clear-headed for prayer, love earnestly, and use each gift to serve others.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Neighbours were baffled when converts no longer joined them, and spoke against them.

Now: Love covers a multitude of sins: it does not pass offences around.

verseByVerse.quote: Since therefore Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same way of thinking, for whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin, so as to live for the rest of the time in the flesh no longer for human passions but for the will of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since Christ suffered in the flesh, believers must arm themselves with the same resolve and live for God’s will.

Armed with a thought. The weapon is a settled conviction: suffering is the road Christ took. Decide what suffering means before it comes, not during it.

“Ceased from sin”. Not that suffering makes us sinless; the commands that follow assume otherwise. Some refer it to Christ, who is done with sin after dealing with it once (3:18). More likely, it describes what suffering for Christ does to a believer: he has chosen under pressure, and the choice settles something. He has stopped negotiating with sin.

On a Tuesday. A young man loses a promotion because he refused to falsify figures. It hurt. But the pull of that kind of success has lost its grip on him. He has learnt what it was worth.

verseByVerse.quote: For the time that is past suffices for doing what the Gentiles want to do, living in sensuality, passions, drunkenness, orgies, drinking parties, and lawless idolatry. With respect to this they are surprised when you do not join them in the same flood of debauchery, and they malign you;
verseByVerse.commentary:
They have spent enough time living like pagans, who are surprised when believers no longer join them.

Enough. A dry understatement: you have given that more than enough of your life.

A social list. Every item was done in company, and much of it was part of temple worship. Leaving it cost friends.

Surprised. The neighbours are bewildered. When everyone is carried by a current, the one standing still feels like a criticism of all the others.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians must avoid unbelievers’ social occasions. Jesus ate with sinners (Luke 7:34), and we cannot leave the world (1 Corinthians 5:10). The issue is joining the excess. You may be at the party; you should not be part of what it becomes.

On a Tuesday. A new Christian stops going to Friday binges with his workmates. They tease him and stop inviting him. Peter would tell him to keep loving them, invite them to something else, and expect questions. Their surprise is an opening.

verseByVerse.quote: but they will give account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead. For this is why the gospel was preached even to those who are dead, that though judged in the flesh the way people are, they might live in the spirit the way God does.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who malign them will give account to God, who judges the living and the dead.

Ready. The Judge is standing by. The delay is patience, not absence.

Preached to the dead? Some early writers read this as preaching to the dead in Hades, or link it with 3:19. The most likely reading is that the gospel was preached to believers while they were alive who have since died. Neighbours mocked: “Their faith did them no good; they died like everyone else.” Peter answers: they died, the judgment all flesh receives, but they live with God. Scripture gives no second chance after death (Hebrews 9:27).

For worship. At a Christian funeral, this verse speaks. Death passed its verdict on the body. It did not have the last word.

verseByVerse.quote: The end of all things is at hand; therefore be self-controlled and sober-minded for the sake of your prayers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The end of all things is near, so be sober-minded for prayer.

The end. Telos: not merely the stopping but the goal. Things will not run out; they will arrive.

“At hand”. Two thousand years have passed. The New Testament never set a date; it called the church to live in readiness. Peter knew that with the Lord a day is as a thousand years (2 Peter 3:8).

A steady head. We might expect a call to dramatic action. Peter says: be sober and pray. A frightened, distracted or intoxicated mind cannot pray.

On a Tuesday. Most prayer fails not through unbelief but through clutter. Turn off the noise for ten minutes, clear your head, and pray. Peter treats that as preparation for the end.

verseByVerse.quote: Above all, keep loving one another earnestly, since love covers a multitude of sins. Show hospitality to one another without grumbling.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Above all, love one another earnestly, and show hospitality without grumbling.

Covers. From Proverbs 10:12. Not atonement (only Christ’s blood does that), and not concealment of crime. It means love does not spread offences, rehearse them or keep the account open. Small, persecuted churches meeting in homes produced constant friction; love decided whether they survived it.

What it does not mean. Love overlooks many small wrongs and forgives readily. But serious or unrepentant sin must be confronted (Matthew 18:15–17), and abuse and crime must be reported to the proper authorities (Romans 13:4). Covering sin in love never means hiding harm from those who need protecting.

Hospitality without grumbling. There were no church buildings; someone’s home took the wear, and travelling Christians needed beds. Peter knows the host household is most likely to resent it, and that resentment comes out as muttering.

On a Tuesday. Your small group meets at your house again, and the carpet is wearing. Peter says: open the door, and stop muttering about it. Your home is one of God’s tools.

verseByVerse.quote: As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of God's varied grace: whoever speaks, as one who speaks oracles of God; whoever serves, as one who serves by the strength that God supplies—in order that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ. To him belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each believer must use his gift to serve others as a steward of God’s varied grace, so that God is glorified.

Each. Every believer has a gift. And it comes already assigned: for others.

Stewards. We manage what belongs to God and will give account. “Varied” means many-coloured, like embroidered cloth. A church of one colour has lost something God meant to be seen.

Speaking and serving. Word and deed. Those who speak in the church should handle it as God’s own words: carefully, not casually. Those who serve run on God’s supply, not their own reserves.

Prophecy today? Continuationists include prophecy and tongues among the speaking gifts here. Peter’s point is that whoever speaks in the church, teaching, preaching or exhorting, should speak “as one who speaks oracles of God” by faithfully passing on what God has said. The more likely reading is that this describes faithful handling of God’s revealed word, not new revelation.

For worship. Thinking rightly about gifts ends in doxology. The goal is not the gift, but God glorified.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Do not be surprised by the fiery trial, as though something strange were happening. Rejoice as you share Christ’s sufferings. If you are insulted for his name, the Spirit of glory rests on you. Do not suffer as a wrongdoer or a meddler; but if you suffer as a Christian, do not be ashamed. Judgment begins with God’s household. So those who suffer by God’s will should entrust their souls to their faithful Creator and keep doing good.
verseByVerse.theology:
Judgement Beginning at Home

Do not be surprised by the fiery trial. To suffer as a Christian is no shame; entrust your soul to a faithful Creator while doing good.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: “Christian” was probably an outsiders’ insult, and Peter told them to wear it.

Now: Make sure any suffering is for Christ’s name, not for wrongdoing or interfering.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you. But rejoice insofar as you share Christ's sufferings, that you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers must not be surprised by fiery trials, but rejoice to share Christ’s sufferings.

Do not be surprised. The same word as v. 4. Pagans are surprised at you; do not you be surprised at this.

The fiery trial. Literally “the burning”, the smelting word from 1:7. It has a purpose: to test.

The real danger. Not the suffering but how we read it: concluding that it is abnormal, that God has withdrawn, that others must be doing better. Peter says suffering is a normal part of the Christian life. Much of the pain of suffering is the suspicion that it should not be happening.

Insofar as. Joy is commanded for the share of suffering that is truly a share in Christ’s. And it is one joy in two instalments: begun under the fire, completed when his glory appears.

On a Tuesday. A believer loses friends over her faith and thinks something must be wrong with her. Peter would say: this is normal. Christ walked here first, and you are walking with him.

verseByVerse.quote: If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Insult for Christ’s name is a blessing, for the Spirit of glory rests on them.

For his name. Not for being tactless or difficult. Peter makes that distinction in the next verse.

Insult. Most Christians under pressure face not courts but contempt: a reputation quietly ruined.

The Spirit rests. The verb is from Isaiah 11:2, where the Spirit rests on the Messiah, and it recalls the glory-cloud that rested on the tabernacle. The presence that filled the tent rests on people being sworn at in the street.

A textual note. Some manuscripts add “and of power” after “glory”, and later ones add a sentence found in the KJV: “on their part he is evil spoken of, but on your part he is glorified.” Both are probably later additions. The meaning is unaffected.

verseByVerse.quote: But let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer or as a meddler. Yet if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in that name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No believer should suffer as a wrongdoer, but suffering as a Christian is no shame.

Earned trouble. Peter will not let the blessing of v. 14 be claimed by a Christian who brought trouble on himself.

A meddler. The word may be Peter’s own coinage: someone who oversees other people’s business. Placed beside murder and theft, it is startling. A busybody in a suspected minority does real damage, then mistakes the hostility for persecution.

“Christian”. Used only three times in the New Testament, and probably an outsiders’ nickname first used at Antioch (Acts 11:26). Peter tells them to catch the insult and wear it.

On a Tuesday. Before calling your trouble persecution, ask honestly: is this for Christ, or for my sharp tongue, my laziness, or my interfering? If it is for Christ, do not be ashamed. If it is not, repent.
verseByVerse.note: “Christian” was first a nickname given by outsiders; it appears only three times in the New Testament.

verseByVerse.quote: For it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God; and if it begins with us, what will be the outcome for those who do not obey the gospel of God? And "If the righteous is scarcely saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner?" Therefore let those who suffer according to God's will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judgment begins with God’s household; those who suffer must entrust themselves to their faithful Creator and keep doing good.

Judgment begins at home. The idea comes from Ezekiel 9:6: “begin at my sanctuary”. Their suffering is not outside God’s plan; it is the first movement of his refining, and it starts with his people.

From lesser to greater. Peter leaves the question hanging. If God’s household goes through this, what of those who reject the gospel?

Scarcely saved. From Proverbs 11:31. Not saved by a narrow margin or with barely enough grace, but saved through difficulty. Salvation is certain; the road is hard.

Entrust. The deposit word, as Christ entrusted himself to the Judge (2:23). And God is called Creator, the only time in the New Testament. Hand your soul back to the one who made it. He is faithful; the deposit will be there. And do it “while doing good”: not instead of acting, but while acting.

On a Tuesday. A Christian facing a hostile tribunal at work prays before the meeting: “Faithful Creator, I give you my soul and my reputation.” Then she goes in and does her job well.

4.text: <sup>1</sup>Since therefore Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same way of thinking, for whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin,<sup>2</sup>so as to live for the rest of the time in the flesh no longer for human passions but for the will of God.<sup>3</sup>For the time that is past suffices for doing what the Gentiles want to do, living in sensuality, passions, drunkenness, orgies, drinking parties, and lawless idolatry.<sup>4</sup>With respect to this they are surprised when you do not join them in the same flood of debauchery, and they malign you;<sup>5</sup>but they will give account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead.<sup>6</sup>For this is why the gospel was preached even to those who are dead, that though judged in the flesh the way people are, they might live in the spirit the way God does.<sup>7</sup>The end of all things is at hand; therefore be self-controlled and sober-minded for the sake of your prayers.<sup>8</sup>Above all, keep loving one another earnestly, since love covers a multitude of sins.<sup>9</sup>Show hospitality to one another without grumbling.<sup>10</sup>As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of God's varied grace:<sup>11</sup>whoever speaks, as one who speaks oracles of God; whoever serves, as one who serves by the strength that God supplies—in order that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ. To him belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.<sup>12</sup>Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you.<sup>13</sup>But rejoice insofar as you share Christ's sufferings, that you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed.<sup>14</sup>If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you.<sup>15</sup>But let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer or as a meddler.<sup>16</sup>Yet if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in that name.<sup>17</sup>For it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God; and if it begins with us, what will be the outcome for those who do not obey the gospel of God?<sup>18</sup>And "If the righteous is scarcely saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner?"<sup>19</sup>Therefore let those who suffer according to God's will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good.

5.title: Humble Yourselves: Elders, Community, and the God of All Grace
5.overview: The last chapter has three movements: elders are to shepherd God’s flock (vv. 1–5); the whole church is to humble itself under God’s mighty hand, cast its anxieties on him and resist the devil (vv. 6–11); and closing greetings place the letter in “Babylon”, almost certainly Rome (vv. 12–14). Its climax is one of the finest benedictions in the New Testament: after a little while, the God of all grace will himself restore, confirm, strengthen and establish you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Shepherd the Flock of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter writes to the elders as a fellow elder. Shepherd God’s flock willingly, not under compulsion; eagerly, not for money; by example, not by domineering. When the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive an unfading crown of glory. Younger people should submit to the elders, and everyone should put on humility, because God opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble.
verseByVerse.theology:
Three Temptations and Their Remedies

Elders are to shepherd God's flock willingly, eagerly and by example — not under compulsion, not for gain, not by domineering. The chief Shepherd is coming.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter wrote to elders as a fellow elder, not as an apostle.

Now: Everyone is to tie on the servant’s apron of humility.

verseByVerse.quote: So I exhort the elders among you, as a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, as well as a partaker in the glory that is going to be revealed:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter appeals to the elders as a fellow elder and witness of Christ’s sufferings and partaker of the coming glory.

Fellow elder. He could have written “as an apostle”. Speaking to leaders about leading, he sits in their chair. The word appears nowhere else in the New Testament; he may have coined it.

Witness of the sufferings. He watched from the courtyard, and failed there. The man telling elders to feed the sheep was told three times on a beach to do the same, after denying the Shepherd (John 21:15–17).

Between suffering and glory. He has seen the sufferings and will share the glory. That is where the whole letter places its readers too.

verseByVerse.quote: shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight, not under compulsion, but willingly, as God would have you; not for shameful gain, but eagerly; not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elders must shepherd God’s flock willingly, eagerly and by example, not for gain or domination.

The flock of God. It belongs to God, not the elders, and they are “among” it, not above it. Peter has given the titles Shepherd and Overseer first to Christ (2:25).

Three temptations. Compulsion: serving out of duty or because no one else will. Gain: calculating what the post returns. Domineering: the verb Jesus used of Gentile rulers, “it shall not be so among you” (Mark 10:42–43). Peter was in the room.

Example. Not weak leadership but a harder kind. A man who leads by command only needs to be obeyed; a man who leads by example has to be worth copying.

On a Tuesday. An elder is tired and tempted to resign. Another loves the platform. A third likes controlling decisions. Peter’s three pairs are a mirror for all of them, and for anyone who leads a home group, a youth club or a family.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the chief Shepherd appears, faithful elders will receive an unfading crown of glory.

One chief Shepherd. The word appears nowhere else in the Greek Bible. Every elder is under him. That answers the three temptations at their root: no one serves grudgingly, greedily or harshly when minding someone else’s sheep with the owner due home.

Unfading crown. The victor’s wreath of leaves at the games browned within a week. “Unfading” comes from the amaranth, a flower symbolising what does not wither. The crown consists of glory itself.

What about the papacy? Roman Catholic teaching sees Peter as the first bishop of Rome with authority over the whole church. Here Peter, writing probably from Rome, places himself alongside the elders and points them to Christ as chief Shepherd. Nothing in his letters claims a supreme office or successors.

For worship. Unpaid, unnoticed and often in danger, these elders are promised recognition from the only one whose opinion is final.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, you who are younger, be subject to the elders. Clothe yourselves, all of you, with humility toward one another, for "God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The younger must submit to the elders, and all must clothe themselves with humility, for God gives grace to the humble.

Tie on humility. The verb means to tie on, used of the apron a slave fastened before serving. Peter had watched Jesus tie on a towel and wash feet, and he had objected (John 13:4–8). The picture he chooses is the one he first refused.

God opposes. From Proverbs 3:34 (also James 4:6). A military word: drawn up in battle against. Grace can only be received by open hands, which is why humility is the posture for receiving anything from God.

On a Tuesday. In a church argument over music or money, humility looks like listening first, assuming the best, and being willing to lose. It is the apron Christ wore.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–14 — Cast Your Anxieties, and Stand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter tells his readers to humble themselves under God’s strong hand, so that he will lift them up in due time, and to throw all their worries onto him because he cares for them. They must stay sober and alert, because their enemy the devil prowls like a hungry lion looking for someone to devour; they are to resist him, firm in faith, knowing that believers throughout the world are going through the same sufferings. After they have suffered a little while, the God of all grace, who called them to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore, establish and strengthen them. To him belongs power for ever. Peter adds that he has written briefly through Silvanus to encourage them and testify that this is the true grace of God, and they must stand firm in it. He sends greetings from the church in “Babylon” and from Mark, asks them to greet one another with a kiss of love, and wishes peace to all who are in Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why Worry Is Treated as Pride

Humble yourselves by casting all your anxieties on God, because he cares for you. After a little while, the God of all grace will himself restore you.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The devil prowled like a roaring lion, looking for anyone cut off from the flock.

Now: Resist him, firm in the faith, knowing the same sufferings are shared by believers throughout the world.

verseByVerse.quote: Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you, casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Humble yourselves under God’s mighty hand and cast all your anxieties on him, for he cares for you.

The mighty hand. An exodus phrase. The hand is heavy, and it is the hand that delivers.

His timing. The lifting is his work. Insisting on being raised now takes the job out of the right hands.

Worry as pride. “Casting” is a participle attached to “humble yourselves”: it is how we humble ourselves. Holding on to anxiety insists the situation is ours to manage. Throwing it on God is an act of humility. “All” leaves nothing too small.

Is anxiety a sin? This verse is an invitation, not a rebuke: “he cares for you”. Some anxiety comes from pride and self-reliance and needs to be handed over. Some has bodily causes and is an illness; seeing a doctor or counsellor, or taking medication, is no lack of faith. Bring the burden to God, again and again, and use every means he gives.

He cares. Not only that he can help, but that you matter to him. To people their neighbours treated as nothing, Peter says: you are on God’s mind.

On a Tuesday. Lying awake at 3 a.m., name each worry aloud and throw it on him, one by one. Then say: “You care for me.” You may need to do it again tomorrow night. That is allowed.

verseByVerse.quote: Be sober-minded; be watchful. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. Resist him, firm in your faith, knowing that the same kinds of suffering are being experienced by your brotherhood throughout the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be sober and watchful, for the devil prowls like a roaring lion; resist him, firm in faith.

Watchful. The word from Gethsemane, “watch and pray” (Matthew 26:41), where Peter slept.

Adversary. A courtroom word: the prosecutor. These readers were being accused constantly.

The roar. A stalking lion is silent; the roar is meant to panic the herd and drive one animal out. The devil works on the nerves, seeking “someone”, the one that drifts from the group.

Resist, firm. Stand, do not scatter. Not by bravado, but by faith.

Not alone. Believers everywhere suffer the same things. Isolation is the lion’s method; fellowship is the answer.

On a Tuesday. When you feel low and want to skip church and avoid Christian friends, notice the pattern. That is when the lion hunts. Go anyway. Stay with the flock.

verseByVerse.quote: And after you have suffered a little while, the God of all grace, who has called you to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you. To him be the dominion forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After a little suffering, the God of all grace will restore, confirm, strengthen and establish them.

A little while. The suffering is not removed from the sentence, but it is bounded, measured against eternal glory.

The God of all grace. Grace of every kind, enough for every situation.

Four verbs. Restore: the word for setting a broken bone or mending nets, which Peter did for a living. Confirm: the word Jesus used when he told Peter to strengthen his brothers after he turned back (Luke 22:32). Strengthen. Establish: set on a foundation.

Himself. God will do the mending personally. Peter had been broken and restored by name.

For worship. Peter has just named the prowling lion. He ends by saying whose the dominion really is.

verseByVerse.quote: By Silvanus, a faithful brother as I regard him, I have written briefly to you, exhorting and declaring that this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it. She who is at Babylon, who is likewise chosen, sends you greetings, and so does Mark, my son. Greet one another with the kiss of love. Peace to all of you who are in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter closes, affirming that this is the true grace of God, and sends greetings.

Silvanus. The Silas of Acts, Paul’s companion, perhaps also Peter’s scribe, which may explain the letter’s polished Greek.

The true grace of God. After five chapters on suffering, submission and slander, Peter calls it all grace. Their part is to stand in it.

Babylon. Almost certainly Rome. Jewish writers used the name for the pagan power that destroyed Jerusalem, and Revelation does the same. Even the church at the empire’s centre is in exile. “Likewise chosen” returns to the letter’s first word (1:1).

Mark. John Mark, who once deserted Paul and was restored. Early tradition says he wrote his Gospel from Peter’s preaching.

The kiss. The point is warm, holy affection, expressed in whatever form a culture uses. A handshake or an embrace obeys the command where a kiss would mean something else.

Peace. The letter ends with peace, offered to people with little of it, by a man who would soon die in the city he calls Babylon.
verseByVerse.note: Silvanus is the Silas of Acts. “Babylon” is very probably a code name for Rome. Mark is John Mark, whom early tradition links with Peter as the source of Mark’s Gospel.
